sharedText: the word of the Lord came to me by
reason: A five-word run and the chapter's only candidate at this verse, and it is the standing prophetic formula. 'The word of the LORD came' opens well over a hundred KJV verses; that 1 Kings 13:17 is the one the n-gram stream surfaced is an accident of the following preposition, not a signal. The senses are also unrelated: 1 Kings 13:17 is the old prophet's lie to the man of God about eating bread at Bethel, and Moroni 8:7 is Mormon reporting a genuine revelation. The substantive borrowing in this sentence is the Acts 15 shape of inquiring upward about a disputed rite, adjudicated at Moroni 8:5.

Ranked on a four-word run that stops one word before the word that matters. Galatians 1:21 reads 'Afterwards I came into the regions of Syria and Cilicia' — a travel itinerary. Moroni 8:8's 'I came into the world' is Christ speaking of the incarnation, and the KJV verse that actually holds that phrase is 1 Timothy 1:15, 'Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners', which is entered as a composite on the Luke 5:31 link at this verse. The pilot's 'window closes one word early' trap (ADJUDICATING §4) in its plainest form.

The chapter's second-highest candidate at this verse on a five-word run, and the sense could hardly be more opposed. Jeremiah 44:12 is the oracle against the remnant of Judah who fled to Egypt: 'they shall all be consumed, and fall in the land of Egypt… by the sword and by the famine'. Moroni 8:10 is 'they shall all be saved with their little children'. Same four words, opposite verb, and the verb is the whole content. Nothing else of Jeremiah 44 is present — no Egypt, no remnant, no sword, no famine — and 'they shall all be' is ordinary English besides. Recorded because a long run at a chapter's doctrinal climax is exactly the kind of match a careless reader accepts.

A five-word run ranked at both 8:10 and 8:14, and it is the Book of Mormon's most common speech formula as well as one of the KJV's. 'I say unto you' stands in well over two hundred KJV verses; John 4:35's harvest saying has nothing to do with baptism, children, or accountability, and shares no other word with either verse. This entry covers the same candidate at Moroni 8:14 and is not repeated there.

A four-word run and a genuine trap, because 'from the foundation of the world' is a real biblical phrase and Moroni 8:12 uses it. But 1 Kings 7:9's 'foundation' is masonry — 'costly stones… sawed with saws, within and without, even from the foundation unto the coping' — in a description of Solomon's building works, and its 'even from the foundation' is followed by 'unto the coping', not 'of the world'. The phrase Moroni 8:12 actually has occurs in six KJV verses (Matthew 13:35, 25:34, Luke 11:50, Hebrews 4:3, 9:26, Revelation 13:8) and is too common to identify a source; the verse's real borrowing is 1 Corinthians 15:22, adjudicated at this verse.

'For he hath neither faith, hope, nor charity' is 1 Corinthians 13:13's triad in Moroni's own order, and it is a real borrowing — but it is the borrowing this book has already made, at Moroni 7:1, in the same author's sermon a few pages earlier, and 7:44-46 quote the surrounding chapter of 1 Corinthians outright. This is Mormon reusing his own adopted formula within one book (ADJUDICATING §4), so the argument is made there and this occurrence is cross-referenced rather than re-argued. The fresh borrowing at 8:14 is Acts 8:23, adjudicated at this verse.

A five-word run built entirely out of 'after this manner', which the KJV uses in some forty verses and the Book of Mormon constantly. Jeremiah 13:9 is 'After this manner will I mar the pride of Judah'; the words that follow it in Moroni 8:16 — 'pervert the ways of the Lord' — belong to a different verse entirely, Acts 13:10, which is adjudicated here. The candidate's rarity score is an artifact of the two function-word runs overlapping.

Moroni 8:17's 'I am filled with charity, which is everlasting love' and 'I love little children with a perfect love' are the chapter's densest charity language, and a reader arriving at this verse is entitled to be told where it is adjudicated. It is Moroni 7:44-48, where Mormon's sermon quotes 1 Corinthians 13:2, 13:4 and 13:8 verbatim and glosses charity as 'the pure love of Christ' — the same author, the same book, the same definition. The one element at 8:17 that is not from that block is 'perfect love', which comes from 1 John 4:18 and is adjudicated at Moroni 8:16.

The highest-ranked candidate at this verse, on a six-word run, and the source is right — 'the power of his redemption' is built on Philippians 3:10's 'the power of his resurrection'. But that borrowing is adjudicated at Moroni 7:41, where the same author writes 'the power of his resurrection' with the noun unchanged, and 8:20 is his own phrase reused with a substitution. Within one book a repeat is not a fresh borrowing (ADJUDICATING §4); a reader is sent from here to 7:41.

'Setteth at nought the atonement of him' is genuinely Romans 14:10's 'why dost thou set at nought thy brother' — but the link is written at Moroni 8:21, one verse later, because that is where the second and rarer half of Romans 14:10 lands: 'stand before the judgment seat of Christ' is a KJV singleton and Moroni 8:21 has it. The two verses together reproduce one KJV verse in its own order, so the row sits where the argument can be made whole. See Moroni 8:21.

A four-word run of pure connective tissue. 2 John 1:1's 'all they that have known the truth' is the elder's greeting to a congregation; Moroni 8:22's 'all they that are without the law' is a doctrinal category drawn from Romans 2:12 and 5:13, which are adjudicated at this verse. Noted rather than passed over in silence only because 2 John does bear on this chapter — at 8:30, where its closing formula is a genuine candidate — and a reader should not confuse the two.

'Meekness, and lowliness of heart' is Matthew 11:29's 'I am meek and lowly in heart', the KJV's one occurrence of the pair, and it is a real borrowing. It is adjudicated at Moroni 7:43, in the same book and the same author's hand, where the 1830/1920 evidence for it is set out in full — the 1830's 'lowly of heart' against the KJV's 'in heart', and 1920's inconsistent correction back toward the source. 8:26 is Mormon reusing his own phrase, and is cross-referenced rather than re-argued.

A four-word run, and the temptation is that both phrases name the Lord's own words as a standard: 1 Timothy 6:3's 'consent not to wholesome words, even the words of our Lord Jesus Christ', Moroni 8:29's 'the words of our Saviour himself'. But the shared string is four function words plus a possessive, the titles differ ('Saviour' against 'Lord Jesus Christ'), and 1 Timothy 6:3 is about teachers of another doctrine while Moroni 8:29 is about a nation about to be destroyed for rejecting what it already knows. The verse's argument comes from Hebrews 2:3, adjudicated here. The other four-word candidates at this verse — Romans 13:10's 'the fulfilling of the', Deuteronomy 1:17's 'as well as the', Isaiah 29:11's 'as the words of' — are connective noise and are passed over in silence.

'And the first fruits of repentance is baptism' invites a New Testament firstfruits reference, and the two candidates are Romans 8:23 ('the firstfruits of the Spirit') and James 1:18 ('a kind of firstfruits of his creatures'). Neither will bear it. The KJV's firstfruits are always an offering or a first instalment of something already possessed, and Moroni 8:25's are the first thing produced by repentance — an ordinal, not an offering. The verse is the middle link of the Hebrews 6:1-2 chain adjudicated at Moroni 8:23, and it is there that its structure is accounted for. Recorded because the phrase looks scriptural and is not.
